name: Mathcore
about: Mathcore is metalcore pushed to the edge of comprehension: tempo and time-signature changes every few bars, dissonant, jazz-derived chords, blast beats, screamed vocals and songs often under two minutes. It took shape in the mid-1990s American hardcore underground, with Deadguy, Coalesce, Botch and Converge each dismantling the hardcore riff in their own way; the term, borrowed from math rock, caught on once The Dillinger Escape Plan's Calculating Infinity in 1999 made the chaos virtuosic. Converge's Jane Doe two years later gave it an emotional core. The 2000s brought a wave of faster, sillier variants from the Locust, Psyopus and the Number Twelve Looks Like You, while Dillinger and Converge grew more melodic. In the 2010s Britain's Rolo Tomassi and Frontierer, and Long Island's Car Bomb, kept the style alive and forbidding.

artists.name: The Dillinger Escape Plan
artists.why: the virtuosos who defined the style

albums.title: Calculating Infinity
albums.why: Forty minutes of jazz-schooled fury, inhuman precision and Dimitri Minakakis's shriek, the record that gave mathcore its name and its ceiling.

albums.title: Jane Doe
albums.why: Kurt Ballou's whiplash riffs and Jacob Bannon's grief turned hardcore chaos into something lasting, and the title track is its twelve-minute cathedral.

albums.title: We Are the Romans
albums.why: Angular, sardonic and surprisingly tuneful, the Tacoma band's second album is the genre's most intelligent record and its most quoted.

albums.title: Miss Machine
albums.why: Greg Puciato's arrival brought singing, Mike Patton-style eclecticism and genuine songs to the band's chaos without diluting it.

albums.title: Axe to Fall
albums.why: Guests from Cave In, Neurosis and Genghis Tron join the band's fastest, most metallic record, with Dark Horse and the closing Steve Von Till duet as bookends.

albums.title: 0:12 Revolution in Just Listening
albums.why: Sean Ingram's roar and Jes Steineger's swinging, Zeppelin-warped riffs on the Kansas City band's wildest and most influential album.

albums.title: Fixation on a Co-Worker
albums.why: The only album by the New Jersey quintet is a dissonant, sarcastic precursor whose influence far outstrips its sales.

albums.title: American Nervoso
albums.why: Rawer than We Are the Romans but already full of stop-start riffs and odd meters, the band's debut set the Pacific Northwest template.

albums.title: Give Them Rope
albums.why: A debut of lurching, low-tuned hardcore so dense it was later remixed and reissued twice; the roots of the style in rough form.

albums.title: Until Your Heart Stops
albums.why: Boston teenagers writing dizzying, Slayer-fast metalcore with Stephen Brodsky's early singing, before the band left for space rock.

albums.title: Protestant
albums.why: New Jersey hardcore stretched into Voivod-style dissonance and sludge, a record that mapped the territory before it had a name.

albums.title: 300 Percent Density
albums.why: Brooklyn's Candiria wove jazz fusion, hip-hop and metallic hardcore together on their most focused and listenable album.

albums.title: Bless the Martyr and Kiss the Child
albums.why: Christian metalcore from Georgia with Botch-style dissonance and a sprawling closer, the record that launched the Solid State generation.

albums.title: Plague Soundscapes
albums.why: Twenty-three songs in twenty-one minutes of synth-squealing, insectile grind from San Diego, mathcore at its most absurd and abrasive.

albums.title: Ideas of Reference
albums.why: Christopher Arp's impossible guitar lines and a general air of lunacy on the Rochester band's debut, a cult object for technique obsessives.

albums.title: Hell Songs
albums.why: Alexis Marshall's drunken-lounge-singer delivery over scraping, sliding guitars made the Providence band's second album a disturbing, genuinely new thing.

albums.title: Minus the Herd
albums.why: The Montreal band added death-metal weight and Meshuggah-style grooves to their mathcore, pointing toward deathcore and djent at once.

albums.artist: The Number Twelve Looks Like You
albums.title: Mongrel
albums.why: New Jersey's shape-shifters mix grind, salsa and jazz on a record whose genre jumps are part of the point.

albums.title: Board Up the House
albums.why: Synthesizers and a drum machine replace a rhythm section on the Philadelphia trio's cold, apocalyptic and unexpectedly melodic second album.

albums.title: Long Live
albums.why: Josh Scogin's Georgia band recorded live in the studio, with gospel interludes and sheer joy in the mayhem, their most complete album.

albums.title: Orange Mathematics
albums.why: Pedro Sagawe's glitching, pitch-shifted guitars on a self-released debut that pushed mathcore into electronic-sounding extremity.

albums.title: Meta
albums.why: Rhythms that fold in on themselves, Michael Dafferner's clean singing and a grasp of dynamics that most mathcore bands never reach.

albums.title: Time Will Die and Love Will Bury It
albums.why: Eva Korman's shifts from scream to dream-pop over synths and blast beats, the Sheffield band's breakthrough and the genre's most beautiful record.

albums.title: Mirrors
albums.why: Kate Davies's London trio reintroduced Dillinger-style ferocity to a new decade with a debut that earned serious attention across the press.
